title: Engineering professional practice
summary: One principle governs everything here: hold the safety, health and welfare of the PUBLIC paramount — and duties to client and employer, though real, are subordinate to it. Most ethics questions are a conflict between the two, and the answer is the public interest. On a conflict of interest, the duty is to DISCLOSE and WITHDRAW, not to proceed carefully; on non-compliant work, to refuse to certify and report it. The test worth carrying is whether the decision would survive disclosure.

sections.heading: The engineering profession and its obligations
sections.body:
**What makes engineering a PROFESSION** rather than merely a skilled occupation:

| Characteristic | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Specialised knowledge** | Acquired by extended formal education |
| **Extensive training** | Practical experience under supervision |
| **A code of ETHICS** | Self-imposed standards beyond legal minimums |
| **Service to SOCIETY** | The work affects public welfare |
| **Registration or licensing** | Entry controlled by a professional body |
| **Autonomy and judgement** | Decisions are exercised, not merely executed |
| **Accountability** | To the profession and to the public |

**The bargain implicit in professional status** is worth stating explicitly, because it explains everything that follows:

> Society grants the profession a **monopoly on certain work, and the autonomy to exercise judgement**. In return, the profession undertakes to **place the public interest above its members' own** — and to **discipline those who do not**.

That is the reason a professional body exists, the reason registration is mandatory, and the reason a code of ethics is enforceable rather than aspirational. An engineer who treats the code as optional is taking the privileges of the bargain while declining its obligation.

**THE FUNDAMENTAL CANON**, common to every engineering code of ethics in the world:

> **Engineers shall hold PARAMOUNT the SAFETY, HEALTH and WELFARE of the PUBLIC in the performance of their professional duties.**

**The word PARAMOUNT is doing the work.** The engineer's duties to the **client** and to the **employer** are real and important — but they are **SUBORDINATE**. Where they conflict, **the public interest prevails**, and it prevails without further argument.

Almost every ethics question set in this subject is a version of that conflict, and recognising the pattern answers most of them.

**The other fundamental canons** (NSPE and ASCE formulations, mirrored in the NEC code):

| Canon | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Perform services only in areas of COMPETENCE** | Do not undertake work beyond your training and experience |
| **Issue public statements only in an OBJECTIVE and TRUTHFUL manner** | No misleading claims; disclose any interest when speaking publicly |
| **Act as a FAITHFUL AGENT or trustee** for each employer or client | Loyalty within the bounds of the first canon |
| **AVOID DECEPTIVE ACTS** | No misrepresentation of qualifications, experience or facts |
| **Conduct yourself HONOURABLY**, so as to enhance the honour and reputation of the profession | — |
| **Continue PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT**, and assist the development of those under your supervision | Competence is not permanent |
| **Give CREDIT** where due | Acknowledge the work of others |
| Uphold **SUSTAINABILITY** in the performance of duties | Increasingly explicit in modern codes |

**Practising only within competence** deserves emphasis because it is easy to violate with good intentions: a competent structural engineer asked to advise on geotechnical matters, or a road engineer asked to certify a water supply design, may be tempted to help. The correct response is to **decline, or to obtain and rely on competent assistance and say so**. A signature carries a representation of competence, and giving one falsely is a disciplinary matter regardless of the outcome.

**Continuing professional development** is a canon rather than a courtesy, and the reason is that **competence decays**: codes are revised, materials change, methods are superseded, and an engineer working to a code withdrawn twenty years ago is not practising competently however diligent they are. NBC 105 was revised in 2020, IRC 37 in 2018, IS 800 in 2007 — an engineer unaware of those is out of date in a way that matters.

sections.heading: Ethical problems and how to reason about them
sections.body:
**CONFLICT OF INTEREST.**

> A conflict of interest exists where an engineer's **personal or financial interest could influence, or could reasonably APPEAR to influence, their professional judgement**.

**The duty is to DISCLOSE and WITHDRAW.**

| Response | Correct? |
|---|---|
| **Disclose the interest and withdraw** from the decision | **CORRECT** |
| Proceed, but carefully and objectively | **Wrong** — objectivity cannot be self-certified |
| Proceed but keep the interest confidential | **Wrong, and worse** — concealment compounds the fault |
| Proceed but reduce the fee | **Wrong** — it does not cure the conflict |

**Why disclosure and withdrawal, rather than careful proceeding.** The problem is **not** that the engineer will necessarily decide wrongly — they may well decide correctly. The problem is that **the affected parties cannot know that**, and are deprived of the ability to judge for themselves. Concealment removes their choice; disclosure restores it.

**The appearance matters as much as the fact**, which is why the test is whether the interest **could reasonably appear** to influence judgement. Public confidence in professional decisions depends on their being visibly disinterested.

Examples: evaluating a tender from a company in which one holds shares, or which employs a family member; specifying a proprietary product from which one receives a commission; accepting substantial gifts or hospitality from a supplier; taking private work that competes with one's employer.

**CERTIFICATION of non-compliant work.**

> Certification is a **PROFESSIONAL REPRESENTATION** that the work conforms to the specification. Certifying work **known** to be non-compliant is a **FALSE STATEMENT** — and one on which the employer, future owners and the public will rely.

**The correct course:**

1. **RECORD** the non-compliance factually — measurements, photographs, date.
2. **NOTIFY** the contractor and the employer **in writing**.
3. **WITHHOLD** the certificate and the associated payment for that work.
4. Require **RECTIFICATION** — or a formally justified, documented and **signed engineering assessment** if the departure can be accepted on technical grounds.
5. If overruled, **ESCALATE** — and if the matter concerns **safety**, report it to the authority concerned.

**Why the softer options fail:**

| Option | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Certify because **the client has accepted** it | The client **cannot waive** a standard that protects **third parties and future occupants** |
| Certify but keep a **private note** | The **certificate** is what others rely on; the note protects the engineer's conscience, not the public. It is arguably **worse**, because it **proves the engineer knew** |
| Certify if the defect **does not affect appearance** | Compliance concerns **performance and safety**, not appearance |

**That last point deserves expansion**, because it is the substance of why certification exists at all: the defects that matter most in construction — **inadequate cover, poor compaction, missing links, wrong bar placement, an omitted DPC** — are precisely the ones that become **INVISIBLE once the work is complete**. Certification exists because they cannot be inspected later. An engineer who certifies work they know to be defective removes the only check the system has.

**Step 4 admits a genuine nuance**: not every departure requires demolition. A non-compliance may be acceptable if a **competent engineering assessment** shows the work still meets its **performance** requirements — but that assessment must be **explicit, documented and signed**, not an informal accommodation. The distinction is between an engineering decision and a quiet concession.

**WHISTLEBLOWING** — external disclosure of wrongdoing.

**It is justified when four conditions are met:**

| Condition | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Serious harm** | The wrong threatens **substantial harm** to the public |
| **Internal channels exhausted** | The engineer has **reported it internally** and been ignored or overruled |
| **Documented evidence** | Not suspicion — **evidence** a reasonable person would find convincing |
| **Reasonable prospect** | Disclosure is likely to **prevent the harm** |

**The sequence matters, and internal escalation comes FIRST:**

> **Record → notify in writing → escalate within the organisation → escalate to the client or the regulator → and only then externally.**

Going public prematurely damages the engineer's standing, exposes them to legal action, and — most importantly — **rarely fixes the problem**, because an organisation given no opportunity to correct itself becomes defensive. Whistleblowing is a **last resort with a high personal cost**, and the engineer who reaches it should have a documented trail showing every earlier step was taken.

**A FRAMEWORK for reasoning about an ethical problem**, which is more useful than memorising cases:

1. **Establish the FACTS.** Many apparent ethical dilemmas dissolve when the facts are clear.
2. **Identify the STAKEHOLDERS** and what each stands to gain or lose.
3. **Identify the ETHICAL ISSUES** and which canons apply.
4. **Consider the ALTERNATIVES** — there are almost always more than two.
5. **Apply TESTS** (below).
6. **Decide, ACT, and DOCUMENT.**

**The tests worth carrying:**

| Test | Question |
|---|---|
| **The PUBLICITY (disclosure) test** | **Would I be comfortable if this decision were reported publicly, with my name on it?** |
| The **reversibility** test | Would I accept this decision if I were the party affected? |
| The **universality** test | Would it be acceptable if **every** engineer did this? |
| The **harm** test | Who is harmed, how seriously, and can it be avoided? |
| The **professional** test | What would a respected, experienced colleague do? |
| The **legal** test | Is it lawful? (necessary, but **NOT sufficient**) |

**The PUBLICITY test is the most useful single heuristic**, and it maps directly onto the conflict-of-interest rule: **if certifying, accepting or concealing something would embarrass you were the facts later known, do not do it.**

**And the legal test is necessary but not sufficient**, which is the point of having a code at all: **an action can be perfectly lawful and still be professionally wrong.** Codes of ethics exist precisely to occupy the space above the legal minimum, and an engineer who asks only "is this legal?" has misunderstood what profession means.

sections.heading: Professional liability, responsibility and the wider duties
sections.body:
**Sources of an engineer's liability:**

| Source | Basis | To whom |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTRACT** | Breach of the terms of engagement | The **client** |
| **TORT (negligence)** | Breach of a **duty of care** causing loss | Anyone to whom a duty is owed — **including third parties** |
| **STATUTE** | Breach of a statutory duty (building code, labour law, environment law) | The state |
| **CRIMINAL** | Where a failure causes death or injury | The state |
| **DISCIPLINARY** | Professional misconduct | The **Nepal Engineering Council** |

**Liability in TORT extends beyond the client**, which is the important point: a duty of care is owed to anyone who might **foreseeably** be harmed by negligent work — future occupants, neighbours, passers-by. A contractual limitation of liability agreed with the client does **not** bind them.

**The standard of care:**

> The **reasonable skill and care of a COMPETENT engineer** in that field — **NOT perfection**, and not the highest conceivable standard.

An engineer is not liable merely because something failed. They are liable if they **fell below the standard a competent practitioner would have met**. Conversely, following accepted practice is a strong defence — though not an absolute one, since a practice can itself be negligent.

**Where a higher standard applies:** an engineer **holding themselves out as a specialist** is judged by the standard of that speciality, and one undertaking a **design and build** obligation may owe a **fitness for purpose** duty, which is stricter than reasonable skill and care because it guarantees a result rather than a standard of effort.

**Managing liability:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Competence** — work within it | Prevents the breach |
| **Documentation** — records, calculations, correspondence, decisions | The evidence that care was taken |
| **Peer review and checking** | Catches errors |
| **Clear scope of engagement** | Defines what was and was not undertaken |
| **Professional indemnity insurance** | Covers the **civil** exposure |
| Limitation of liability clauses | Limited effect; do not bind third parties |

**Insurance covers the civil exposure only.** It does **not** remove **disciplinary** liability to the Council, nor **criminal** liability. That distinction is worth holding: an insured engineer whose negligence killed someone is still liable to lose their registration and to be prosecuted.

**Documentation deserves emphasis** because it is the practical difference between defensible and indefensible work. **Calculations, assumptions, design decisions, site instructions, non-conformance records and the reasons for departures** are the evidence that professional care was exercised. Undocumented care is, in a dispute years later, indistinguishable from none.

**RESPONSIBILITY, ACCOUNTABILITY and AUTHORITY** — three related ideas that questions distinguish:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Responsibility** | The **obligation to perform** a duty |
| **Accountability** | The **obligation to ANSWER** for its performance |
| **Authority** | The **power to make decisions** and commit resources |

**Responsibility can be delegated; ACCOUNTABILITY cannot.** An engineer who delegates a design to a junior remains **accountable** for it — which is why checking and supervision are professional duties rather than administrative conveniences. And **authority must match responsibility**: holding a person responsible for an outcome they lack the authority to affect is both unfair and ineffective.

**PROFESSIONAL RELATIONSHIPS:**

| With | Duties |
|---|---|
| **Client** | Competent service, honest advice, **confidentiality**, disclosure of conflicts, fair fees — **subject always to the public interest** |
| **Employer** | Faithful service, protection of proprietary information, honest reporting |
| **Colleagues** | **Credit where due**, no false criticism, support of juniors, fair competition |
| **Contractors and suppliers** | Fair and impartial dealing, prompt certification, **no acceptance of gifts** |
| **The public** | **Paramount** duty to safety, health and welfare; truthful public statements |
| **The profession** | Uphold its standing; report serious misconduct |

**Confidentiality has a limit**, and it is the same limit as everything else: an engineer may not maintain confidentiality where doing so would **conceal a danger to the public**. That is not an exception to the duty of confidence so much as a consequence of the first canon outranking it.

**Criticism of another engineer's work** requires care: it must be **objective, factual and made in the proper forum**, and the other engineer should generally be **informed**. Disparaging a colleague's work to win an appointment is a disciplinary matter; giving an honest technical opinion when properly asked is a duty.

**SUSTAINABILITY and the wider obligations**, increasingly explicit in modern codes:

| Obligation | Content |
|---|---|
| **Sustainable development** | Meeting present needs **without compromising the ability of future generations** to meet theirs |
| **Environmental protection** | Minimise resource use, waste and pollution; comply with and go beyond the legal minimum |
| **Resource efficiency** | Materials, energy, water, land |
| **Climate** | Mitigation (emissions) and **adaptation** (designing for the climate that will exist, not the one recorded) |
| **Social responsibility** | Consider the affected community; equitable distribution of benefit and harm |
| **Whole-life thinking** | Design for durability, maintainability, and eventual reuse or demolition |

**Adaptation deserves note for Nepal**: designing a bridge or a drain for the rainfall record of the last fifty years assumes that record describes the next fifty, which is increasingly doubtful. Designing for the **climate that will exist** — more intense rainfall, changed glacier behaviour, altered flow regimes — is becoming part of competent practice rather than a refinement.

**Professional bodies and their functions:**

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **Nepal Engineering Council (NEC)** | **Statutory REGULATOR** — registration, license examination, recognition of qualifications, discipline |
| **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)** | **Voluntary ASSOCIATION** — advocacy, professional development, networking |
| Specialist societies | Discipline-specific knowledge and standards |
| International bodies (FIDIC, ICE, ASCE) | International practice and standards |

**The regulator/association distinction** — treated fully in the next subchapter — turns on **whose interest each serves**: a **regulator protects the PUBLIC**, an **association advances its MEMBERS**. Both are legitimate, and confusing them is the error.

**A closing observation on why any of this matters practically.** An engineer's decisions are made **in private, understood by few, and their consequences appear years later**. No client can verify the adequacy of a foundation design; no occupant can inspect the reinforcement in a beam. The whole system therefore depends on the engineer's **own integrity**, backed by the profession's willingness to enforce it. That is not a sentimental observation but a structural one — it is why the ethical obligation is as much a part of professional competence as the calculation.
